<explanation>
Based on the provided file tree and README, here is a detailed explanation for drawing an accurate and comprehensive system design diagram for FastAPI-MCP, a tool that automatically exposes FastAPI endpoints as MCP tools with zero configuration:

1. Project Overview & Purpose:
   • This is a Python package that integrates with a FastAPI application to automatically discover FastAPI endpoints and convert them into MCP tools.
   • The goal is to allow users to “mount” an MCP server onto their FastAPI app, making all endpoints available via the MCP protocol (using Server-Sent Events or a provided proxy, for example).
   • It also supports adding custom tools via decorators.

2. Main Components to Represent:
   • FastAPI Application:
     - This represents the existing FastAPI app (provided by users) to which the MCP functionality is added.
   • MCP Server Module:
     - Represents the core integration logic found in fastapi_mcp/server.py. This module is responsible for setting up and running the MCP server on a specified mount path.
   • HTTP Tools & Conversion Logic:
     - Found in fastapi_mcp/http_tools.py. This component is responsible for the automatic discovery of FastAPI endpoints, converting request/response models, documentation, and schemas into MCP tools.
   • MCP Tools (Auto-generated and Custom):
     - Two aspects: the auto-generated MCP tools (turned from FastAPI endpoints) and additionally defined custom tools (as shown in the README’s advanced usage example with the @mcp_server.tool() decorator).
   • External MCP Clients and Proxies:
     - Clients like Cursor or using mcp-proxy that interact with the MCP server either through SSE or stdio. They are external to the FastAPI app but need to be represented as consumers of the MCP service.

3. Relationships and Interactions:
   • The FastAPI Application integrates (via a call to add_mcp_server) with the MCP Server module. Show an arrow from “FastAPI App” to “MCP Server” indicating the mounting process.
   • The MCP Server, in turn, uses the HTTP Tools module to scan and automatically convert FastAPI endpoints into MCP tools. Use arrows to represent this conversion and data flow.
   • Both auto-generated and custom MCP tools become components available to external clients. Graphically represent a two-way arrow between “MCP Server” and “External MCP Clients” (indicating data flow for API discovery and requests/responses).
   • Optionally, indicate the role of configuration (via setup.py, pyproject.toml, and uv.lock/uv configuration) as supporting modules for deployment and integration.

4. Architectural Patterns and Technologies:
   • The design uses a “zero configuration” integration pattern—simply adding the MCP layer to an existing FastAPI instance without the need for manual endpoint configuration.
   • Emphasize the auto-discovery mechanism:
       – Illustrate how FastAPI endpoints (with their request/response schemas and Swagger-style documentation) are mapped to MCP tool representations.
   • Highlight the use of FastAPI for the backend, Python 3.10+, and support tools like “uv” for dependency installation.
   • Also, include mention of SSE (Server-Sent Events) and alternative stdio methodologies for client connections.

5. Guidelines for Creating the Diagram:
   • Start with separate boxes for:
       - The FastAPI Application (user’s primary API server)
       - The MCP Integration Layer (encompassing fastapi_mcp/server.py and fastapi_mcp/http_tools.py)
       - MCP Tools (with subdivisions for auto-generated and custom tools)
       - External Components (MCP Clients and MCP Proxy, e.g., Cursor and mcp-proxy)
   • Use directional arrows:
       - From FastAPI App to MCP Server (showing the mounting of the MCP endpoint)
       - From MCP Server to HTTP Tools (displaying the discovery and conversion process)
       - From MCP tools to External MCP Clients (data flow for tool discovery and interaction)
   • Incorporate clear labels:
       - Label each box with its role (for example, “FastAPI Application”, “MCP Server”, “HTTP Tools & Converter”, “MCP Tool Repository”, “External MCP Clients”).
   • Use color coding or distinct shapes:
       - For example, one color for core integration modules (MCP Server and HTTP Tools), another for user-defined/custom tools, and a third for external entities.
   • Optionally, add annotations for configuration:
       - Indicate that components such as setup.py, pyproject.toml, and documentation (in README) govern deployment and runtime behavior.

6. Tailoring the Diagram to FastAPI-MCP:
   • Emphasize the integration aspect, showing how the MCP server “attaches” to FastAPI without extra configuration.
   • Highlight the core design principle: automatic discovery. Illustrate with a component that “scans” FastAPI endpoints and “maps” them to MCP tool representations.
   • Make sure to include deployment and connectivity details:
       - Show how users or clients connect, either directly via SSE (URL endpoint like /mcp) or through an intermediary proxy.
       - Represent the optional extension path where developers can add custom MCP tools.

By capturing these essential elements—components, interactions, and technologies—you will produce a detailed system design diagram that reflects both the architecture and the core functionalities of FastAPI-MCP. The diagram should clearly demarcate internal processing (conversion and tool exposure) and external interactions (client communications and integrations) to provide a full picture of how the project operates within a larger ecosystem.
</explanation>
